label: Cyclical Monotonicity and Kantorovich Duality
notes: This central chapter, printed pages 51 to 92, turns optimality into a finite certificate. We meet two faces of the same fact: the support of an optimal plan admits no improving reshuffle, and the minimal cost equals a supremum over price functions. Keep asking which object is fixed and which is optimized.

label: The Monge-Kantorovich Problem
notes: Recall the relaxed problem: minimize the average cost over couplings whose marginals are the prescribed source and target measures. The plan may split mass, so the feasible set is convex and never empty. This linear structure is exactly what makes a clean duality theory possible, and we exploit it throughout the chapter.

label: c-Cyclical Monotonicity
notes: A set is c-cyclically monotone when no finite cyclic permutation of its matched targets lowers total cost. Spell out the inequality with students: sum the costs along the original pairs, compare to any reshuffle around a cycle, and the original must win. This is the combinatorial heart of optimality.

label: Crossing Can Be Improved
notes: Walk through the two-point swap on the line with quadratic cost. The crossing assignment pays more than the parallel one, so uncrossing strictly improves it. Stress that the improving cycle is a certificate of non-optimality: if you can find one, the plan is not optimal, and optimal supports forbid every such cycle.

label: Support of an Optimal Plan
notes: State the structural theorem: under mild cost assumptions the support of any optimal plan is c-cyclically monotone. Emphasize that this is a pointwise, support-level statement, independent of the measures' densities. It converts a global minimization into a local, checkable geometric condition that later yields the Monge map.

label: Kantorovich Duality
notes: Introduce the dual program: maximize the sum of integrals of two potentials constrained so their pointwise sum never exceeds the cost. The duality theorem asserts equality of the primal infimum and dual supremum. Frame phi and psi as prices a shipper pays at origin and destination under a no-arbitrage ceiling.

label: Potentials and the Constraint
notes: The admissibility constraint phi(x) plus psi(y) at most c(x,y) is the no-arbitrage rule. Show that any feasible potential pair gives a valid bound below the transport cost, so the dual supremum cannot exceed the primal. Duality says these two values actually meet, with no gap between them at all.

label: The c-Transform
notes: Define the c-transform: given psi, the best compatible phi is the infimum over y of c minus psi. Iterating once more yields a c-concave function, and the pair stabilizes. Explain that optimizing one potential pointwise against the other is automatic, so the dual really searches over a single c-concave function.

label: Complementary Slackness
notes: At the optimum the inequality phi plus psi at most c becomes equality exactly on the support of the optimal plan. This is complementary slackness: active transported pairs carry zero dual slack, inactive pairs carry nonnegative slack. The notebook makes this visible as a slack matrix whose zeros mark the optimal edges.

label: Kantorovich Potentials
notes: A maximizing pair is called Kantorovich potentials. They are the prices realizing the duality, unique up to an additive constant on connected supports. Tie them to the slackness slide: the equality set of the potentials is precisely where mass is allowed to travel, so the potentials encode the optimal plan's geometry directly.

label: Quadratic Cost: Brenier
notes: Specialize to half the squared distance. Here c-concavity becomes ordinary convexity after a quadratic shift, and the optimal map is the gradient of a convex function. This is Brenier's theorem, the bridge from duality to a genuine transport map, and the template for the polar factorization studied later.

label: Synthesis and Certificate
notes: Close the loop: cyclical monotonicity of the support, existence of Kantorovich potentials, and complementary slackness are three views of the same optimum. The lab perturbs one cost entry to break monotonicity and watch the certificate fail. Optimality is now a finite, inspectable object rather than an abstract minimization.
